A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any non-zero result is a real signal. Two things probably limit it. First, a correct placement depends on the layer the brick lands on (the highest column under its footprint). Whether the cells at that layer are missing, and whether the gaps below would be sealed, needs information per layer. The starting network squashes the layers into one set of column features before pooling over footprints. Second, the default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples, which is very few to learn a policy. I propose a 2x2 factorial against the starting score: a network that keeps the Z axis (layer-folded) with the default recipe, the same network with a recipe giving more updates, and the starting network with that recipe. This separates the effect of the network from the effect of the recipe at about the same compute per sample (r≈1).

### Round 2
All four runs so far, including the starting architecture, scored 0.000 on dev on both seeds, and training success was also 0. The networks are not just generalising badly; the agent never builds a target exactly even during training. Doubling the number of updates didn't help (r1c2, r1c3), and splitting the layers apart (LayerPool) didn't help either. The results can't tell these apart, so two explanations remain. (1) The agent sees too few samples or learns too slowly. Fewer PPO epochs would trade epochs for 2–3× more environment steps at the same compute. (2) The world note warns that the rules may differ from the description. If the actions are numbered differently from what is stated, a convolution head that scores each grid cell as its own anchor would be misaligned and could never learn. A learned dense head over the flattened features doesn't rely on that numbering, so it guards against this case. This round tests sample count, a dense guard head, and a global-attention trunk.

### Round 3
All 7 runs so far, the starting architecture included, scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That covers the layer-folded head, the conv network with a dense head, the column transformer, 64 to 104 updates, and 3x more samples with 1 epoch. Seed noise cannot explain zeros everywhere. Something systematic is blocking learning. There are two candidates. (1) The world may lay out actions differently from the obs grid, for example flipped or transposed axes, or brick type as the fastest-changing index. The conv heads would then score the wrong cells, and the slow zero-initialised dense head never caught up. (2) Too few optimiser steps, plus too much entropy on about 257 actions. So this round tests the layout guard directly (A), an aggressive recipe on the starting network (B), and a cheap network with global context on that recipe (C). Any score above 0 counts as real signal here.

### Round 4
Nine trials and 18 seeds have all scored exactly 0. That held across the trunk shapes, the action heads that would cope with a different action numbering, 405k-step runs and the recipe changes, and training success was also 0. Noise or a few extra samples cannot explain a result this uniform. My best guess at the cause is that the agent learns to choose DONE straight away. Almost every random placement fills cells outside the target and costs 0.01, so its reward is negative, while DONE scores 0. Early PPO updates therefore raise the DONE logit until episodes end at once, and with 257 actions the entropy bonus of 0.01 cannot restore exploration. Then the agent never learns which placements earn positive reward, and it never sees the +1 for an exact build. This last round tests two remedies: a fixed negative offset on the DONE logit, and a stronger entropy bonus. Any result above 0 beats the starting architecture.
